deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is part of Ramanujan's work on highly composite numbers (HCN). Previous pages derived log p_r / log(1+1/r) = log p_1/log 2 + O(r). This page sets up a comparison argument between two indices r and s.

(A) Representation. Write theta(x) = sum_{p<=x} log p and pi(x) = #{p<=x}. Let N = exp(theta(alpha)+theta(beta)+theta(gamma)+...), i.e. N = prod_i prod_{p<=alpha_i} p. A prime p then has exponent a_p = #{i : p <= alpha_i}. Hence d(N) = prod_p (a_p+1).

The formal product 2^{pi(alpha)} (3/2)^{pi(beta)} (4/3)^{pi(gamma)} ... equals prod_p prod_{i: p<=alpha_i} (1+1/i). The step from here is mine. For each p, the a_p indices i satisfy: the j-th smallest index is >= j. Since 1+1/i decreases in i, the inner product is <= prod_{j=1}^{a_p} (1+1/j) = a_p+1. This gives Ramanujan's d(N) >= 2^{pi(alpha)} (3/2)^{pi(beta)} ...

Equality holds exactly when, for every p, {i : p <= alpha_i} is an initial segment {1,...,a_p}. This is equivalent to pi(alpha_1) >= pi(alpha_2) >= ..., i.e. alpha >= beta >= gamma >= ... up to primes. In that case the product telescopes to a_p+1.

(B) Any N = prod p^{a_p} with nonincreasing exponents, in particular any HCN, can be written this way. Take p_r = the largest prime with exponent >= r, so p_1 >= p_2 >= .... Then N = exp(sum theta(p_i)) and d(N) = 2^{pi(p_1)} (3/2)^{pi(p_2)} (4/3)^{pi(p_3)} ....

(C) Perturbation. Replace p_r by a prime q_r and p_s by a prime q_s: N' = N exp(theta(q_r)+theta(q_s)-theta(p_r)-theta(p_s)). By (A), d(N') >= the formal product for N', which is d(N)(1+1/r)^{pi(q_r)-pi(p_r)} (1+1/s)^{pi(q_s)-pi(p_s)}.

Choose q_r > p_r and q_s < p_s with pi(q_r) = pi(p_r)+n and pi(q_s) = pi(p_s) - floor(n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)). Then the log of the multiplier is n log(1+1/r) - floor(n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)) log(1+1/s) >= 0. So d(N') >= d(N).

Since N is highly composite, every M < N has d(M) < d(N). Hence N' >= N, i.e. theta(q_r)+theta(q_s) >= theta(p_r)+theta(p_s).

(D) Elementary bound: for alpha > beta, theta(alpha)-theta(beta) is a sum of pi(alpha)-pi(beta) terms log p with beta < p <= alpha. So {pi(alpha)-pi(beta)} log beta <= theta(alpha)-theta(beta) <= {pi(alpha)-pi(beta)} log alpha.

'Hence' (continued on the next page): n log q_r >= floor(n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)) log q_s. This is to be turned into a relation between p_r and p_s, generalising the r vs 1 relation of the previous page.
errors: No genuine errors. 'then only d(N) = ...' should be read as 'equality holds (only) when the alpha's are ordered'; strictly this is ordering of pi-values, not of the reals alpha.

Implicit assumptions not stated: the alpha_i, p_i, q_r, q_s are primes (or reals); pi(p_s) - floor(...) >= 0 so that q_s exists (with pi(q_s) = 0 meaning that factor is dropped); and the floor is >= 1 if q_s < p_s is to be strict. All are harmless.
The inequality d(N') >= formal product needs part (A), since after the replacement the q's need not be in nonincreasing order. Ramanujan correctly writes >= here.

results.what: Representation N = exp(sum_i theta(p_i)) with p_i = largest prime of exponent >= i, and d(N) = 2^{pi(p_1)} (3/2)^{pi(p_2)} (4/3)^{pi(p_3)} ...; for an unordered sequence d(N) >= that product
results.modern_name: Ramanujan's theta/pi parametrisation of numbers with nonincreasing exponents (highly composite numbers)
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan, 'Highly composite numbers' (Proc. LMS 1915) and the suppressed part published by Nicolas & Robin (Ramanujan J. 1997)

results.what: Exchange argument: perturb p_r up by n primes and p_s down by floor(n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)) primes, keeping d(N') >= d(N), hence N' >= N, giving inequalities between p_r and p_s
results.modern_name: Ramanujan's comparison method for estimating the largest prime with a given exponent in an HCN (log p_r / log(1+1/r) ~ log p_1 / log 2)
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan 1915 (HCN paper, sections on the exponents of large primes)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the argument in Ramanujan's known HCN work (published 1915, with the suppressed portion published in 1997). The method and notation are known to be his; the page adds only drafting detail.

checkable.asserts: Telescoping: prod_{i=1}^k (1+1/i) = k+1, the basis of the d(N) formula (should give 0).

checkable.asserts: Choice (1) makes the exponent of the multiplier nonnegative, so d(N') >= d(N).
